comparison: Both support the basic observation of 44-kHz vocalizations during fear conditioning (C1, C2, C31-C33). OpenEval provides detailed quantitative assessment with sample sizes and p-values, while peer reviewers accept the observation as 'solid' evidence despite noting low emission rates.

Both support the acoustic characterization (C3-C6, C35-C39). OpenEval notes the 99.8% classification accuracy and large sample size while acknowledging potential circularity in threshold setting. Peer reviewers describe the 'detailed spectrographic analysis' as a strength without raising methodological concerns.

Both support the structural heterogeneity and subtype classification (C7, C71, C74-C75). OpenEval notes the lack of inter-rater reliability reporting for manual sorting, while peer reviewers accept the categorization as part of the 'detailed spectrographic analysis' strength.

Both support the temporal dynamics and progressive emergence pattern (C40-C45). OpenEval provides detailed quantitative assessment noting high individual variability, while peer reviewers acknowledge the observation in response to prolonged conditioning without challenging the temporal patterns.

Both support the context-specificity with independent replication (C51-C53). OpenEval emphasizes the convergent evidence from different laboratories and paradigms, while peer reviewers accept these citations as complementary evidence without challenging the contextualization.

Both support the dynamic changes in call characteristics (C54-C58). OpenEval notes the appropriate reporting of non-significant findings for 44-kHz frequency changes, while peer reviewers accept these temporal dynamics without methodological concerns.

Both support the amplitude analysis with technical corrections (C59-C64). OpenEval highlights the importance of the angle-dependent attenuation correction while noting uncertainty in correction magnitude, while peer reviewers accept the amplitude measurements without raising concerns about the technical adjustments.

Both support the association between 44-kHz calls and freezing behavior (C65-C70). OpenEval notes the multiple temporal resolutions and lack of significant difference from 22-kHz calls, while peer reviewers implicitly accept the behavioral measures as part of the 'solid' evidence.

Both support the frequency ratio relationship and 'supertype group' proposal (C76-C80, C72-C73). OpenEval notes the consistency across analyses but acknowledges the musical interval analogy remains speculative, while peer reviewers accept the classification without challenging the interpretive framework.

Both support the computational validation using clustering approaches (C8, C84-C86). OpenEval notes the relatively low silhouette coefficient (0.198) but emphasizes convergence of methods, while peer reviewers accept the clustering methodology as part of the detailed analysis strength.

Both support the temporal clustering and bout structure analysis (C87-C89). OpenEval notes the use of established criteria and somewhat lower transition probabilities compared to 22-kHz calls, while peer reviewers accept the sequential pattern findings without challenge.

Both support the playback experiment findings (C90-C97, C126-C127). OpenEval notes the dissociation between frequency band and behavioral response while acknowledging potential carry-over effects, while peer reviewers explicitly quote the intermediate response findings without challenging the interpretation.

OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN while peer reviewers SUPPORT the arousal/negative emotional state interpretation (C99-C100, C124). OpenEval emphasizes multiple alternative explanations cannot be ruled out and direct measures are lacking, while peer reviewers implicitly accept the aversive framework without raising alternative interpretations.

Both support the amplitude changes with replication (C111-C113). OpenEval notes the mechanistic interpretation is speculative but appropriately presented, while peer reviewers accept the amplitude measurements as part of the detailed acoustic analysis.

Both support the contextualization from prior literature (C114-C123). OpenEval notes these are primarily literature claims rather than novel findings, while peer reviewers accept the characterization of intensified paradigm and comparative freezing data without dispute.

Both support the explanations for why these calls were not previously characterized (C128-C133, C135-C136). OpenEval suggests the novelty claim may be overstated given prior observations, while peer reviewers accept the novelty assertion and describe the work as 'valuable' without challenging the systematic characterization claim.

Both support the main conclusions and methodological recommendations (C135-C138). OpenEval notes the convergent evidence while emphasizing need for further confirmation, while peer reviewers describe the study as 'valuable' and accept the contribution to the field.

OpenEval evaluates the established knowledge summary (C14-C30) as SUPPORTED with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this background literature review section.

Both support the shared characteristics between call types (C72-C73). OpenEval notes these observations support the supertype proposal, while peer reviewers accept these as part of the frequency ratio relationship without separate evaluation.

OpenEval evaluates the theoretical context citations (C98, C106, C108, C125) as SUPPORTED and accurately represented. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these theoretical framework citations.
